w: What's tested Five of Exam 2's fifty questions come from Exam 1 material: L2, L3, L6 and L10 only How the five break down (from the class, November 11): two from L2, one on which hormones synergize, one on how PTH maintains blood calcium Below: the Exam 1 cram sheet for those four lectures The questions here are the Exam 1 hub's High Likelihood questions for those four lectures (Exam 1's predicted topics) Five questions on Exam 2 are from Exam 1, and only from four of its lectures: L2, L3, L6 and L10. Two come from L2, one asks which hormones work together (synergize) and one asks how PTH keeps blood calcium normal. Here are the key points from those four, in one place. L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary Three hormone types: peptides (stored, surface receptors), amines, steroids (made on demand, cholesterol from LDL, intracellular receptors) Know Gs, Gi, Gq plus the insulin (RTK) and GH (JAK2) receptors Negative feedback is the hallmark: hormonal or physiologic response; short vs long loop Anterior: hypothalamic releasing hormones via the portal system Posterior: makes no hormones; oxytocin and ADH come down axons from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei Dopamine holds prolactin down L3 Endocrinology of Growth Synergy: thyroid hormone (T3) works synergistically with GH on bone growth in children; T3 is on the growth plate slide with GH and IGF-1 GH: somatotrophs, 191 aa, pulses, biggest an hour after sleep onset GHRH (Gs) raises it; somatostatin (Gi, hyperpolarizes) lowers it: yin-yang Also up: ghrelin, sleep, stress; down: IGF-1, GH itself, glucose, free fatty acids Direct (MAPK/ERK, chondrocytes) vs IGF-1 (JAK-STAT, liver) Somatomedin hypothesis: GH needs a serum factor (IGF-1) GH is diabetogenic and lipolytic; builds muscle protein L6 Adrenal Gland Cortex 90% (steroids), medulla (catecholamines); blood flows cortex → medulla Glomerulosa: aldosterone (only zone with aldosterone synthase) Fasciculata/reticularis: cortisol and androgens (DHEA) Lightning bolt 1: cholesterol desmolase, ACTH-driven, rate-limiting for cortisol Angiotensin II (Gq) and high K+ drive aldosterone; ACTH only a little Aldosterone: ENaC + Na/K pump: keep Na, lose K Cortisol turns on PNMT: about 80% epinephrine Addison's: high ACTH + MSH → pigmented gums L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation Synergy: PTH and vitamin D (calcitriol) raise blood calcium together: PTH turns on 1α-hydroxylase, and calcitriol raises gut absorption How PTH maintains blood calcium: bone (through the osteoblasts, which signal the osteoclasts), the kidney (keep calcium, dump phosphate, turn on 1α) and the gut (through calcitriol); net calcium up, phosphate down Low calcium: nerves too excitable → tetany, Trousseau's sign Plasma Ca: 50% ionized, 40% bound, 10% complexed Three sites: gut, bone, kidney Osteoblasts: PTH, D3, estrogen receptors; osteoclasts: calcitonin Skin (UV) → D3; liver → 25-OH; kidney 1α → calcitriol (24 → inactive) 1α on: low Ca, PTH, low phosphate CaSR is Gq; rising intracellular Ca INHIBITS PTH (the paradox) PTH: keep Ca, dump phosphate; bone via osteoblasts; net Ca up, P down PTH receptor on osteoblasts, NOT osteoclasts (osteoclasts are hematopoietic) Primary hyperparathyroidism: high PTH and Ca, low P, kidney stones, more in women
